name: Gideon's ephod
charge: Making an ephod from the spoil; Israel whoring after it
summary: Gideon refused the crown and said the Lord should rule, then asked for the golden earrings of the spoil and made an ephod of them and put it in Ophrah. All Israel went a whoring after it there, and it became a snare to Gideon and his house.
offense: After Midian's defeat, Israel offered Gideon rule for himself, his son, and his son's son. He refused and said the Lord should rule over them (Judges 8:22-23). Those were right words, but the test did not end when he refused the crown. He next asked for the golden earrings from the spoil, and the people willingly spread a garment and cast them into it (Judges 8:24-25). The earrings weighed seventeen hundred shekels of gold, besides other royal ornaments and apparel. Gideon made an ephod and placed it in Ophrah, and all Israel went there a whoring after it (Judges 8:26-27). Spoil taken in the Lord's deliverance was turned into a snare against the Lord's worship. The willingness of the donors did not make the use of their gifts righteous. Gideon had begun by throwing down his father's altar of Baal. Now an object he made drew Israel away (Judges 6:25-27; 8:27). A former act of obedience did not make every later act safe. First Timothy 6:10 warns that the love of money causes men to err from the faith and pierce themselves through with sorrows. The danger of the spoil was what the heart and hands did with it after the battle was won.
judgment: The ephod became a snare to Gideon and his house (Judges 8:27). The man who had refused to replace the Lord as ruler had nevertheless furnished the people with an occasion of unfaithfulness. The judgment is already present in that word, snare: what appeared valuable and honourable caught the household that possessed it. Midian remained subdued and the land rested forty years in Gideon's days (Judges 8:28). Peace did not prove that the ephod was acceptable. Israel could enjoy the fruit of the earlier deliverance while another departure grew among them. A successful past is no measure by which to excuse a present offense. After Gideon's death, Israel returned to Baalim, made Baal-berith their god, forgot the Lord who had delivered them, and showed no kindness to Gideon's house (Judges 8:33-35). Forgetting the Lord and forgetting the service of his deliverer stood together. The history proceeds from a household snare into a national return to false worship. Right words about the Lord's rule must be followed by conduct that keeps the people under that rule.

entries.commentary: The men of Ephraim chode with Gideon sharply: why hast thou served us thus, that thou calledst us not when thou wentest to fight with the Midianites? Ephraim has an attitude because they got called late to the battle and wanted in from the beginning. Gideon answers with wisdom: is not the gleaning of the grapes of Ephraim better than the vintage of Abiezer? God delivered into your hands the princes of Midian, Oreb and Zeeb; what was I able to do in comparison of you? He gave them the best possible situation, the enemy fed right into their hands with nowhere to go, and then their anger was abated toward him.

Gideon and the three hundred pass over Jordan, faint, yet pursuing Zebah and Zalmunna the kings of Midian. He asks the men of Succoth for loaves of bread for his men, and the princes of Succoth answer, are the hands of Zebah and Zalmunna now in thine hand, that we should give bread unto thine army? They try to play neutral ground for fear the kings might come against them if they helped. Gideon promises Succoth that when the Lord has delivered Zebah and Zalmunna into his hand, he will tear their flesh with the thorns of the wilderness and with briers; and when the men of Penuel answer him the same way, he promises to break down their tower when he comes again in peace.

Zebah and Zalmunna were in Karkor with about fifteen thousand men, all that were left of the host of the children of the east, for there fell an hundred and twenty thousand men that drew sword. Three hundred against those numbers: you know God was with them. Gideon went up by the way of them that dwelt in tents and smote the host while it was secure, and when the two kings fled, he pursued and took them, and discomfited all the host.

Returning from battle, Gideon caught a young man of Succoth who described unto him the princes and elders of the city, and he came back to Succoth with Zebah and Zalmunna in hand: behold the kings with whom ye did upbraid me. Gideon and his men had finished off Midian on an empty stomach because of them. He took the elders of the city, and thorns of the wilderness and briers, and with them he taught the men of Succoth; he taught them a lesson, that when the army of the Lord comes through faint and weary and asks for bread, you do not turn them away. And he beat down the tower of Penuel and slew the men of the city.

Zebah and Zalmunna describe the men they slew at Tabor: each one resembled the children of a king. Those were powerful men, and they were Gideon's brethren, the sons of his mother; as the Lord liveth, if ye had saved them alive, I would not slay you. Gideon tells Jether his firstborn, up, and slay them, but the youth drew not his sword, for he feared, because he was yet a youth. We have all had that moment of getting the nudge from pops and being nervous; the son was young, and that is understandable, but you see Gideon being a father, taking his son to the war and teaching him the ways he must walk.

The men of Israel ask Gideon to rule over them, both he, his son, and his son's son, for delivering them from the hand of Midian. Israel has always needed a leader, because we are lost sheep; we need somebody to guide us in the way we must go, or we wander off the path of righteousness. It has always been that way, and you see it playing out right here. Gideon refuses: I will not rule over you, neither shall my son rule over you; the Lord shall rule over you.

Gideon requests of every man the earrings of his prey, for the enemy had golden earrings because they were Ishmaelites; and they willingly gave them, a thousand and seven hundred shekels of gold, beside the ornaments, collars, purple raiment, and camel chains of the kings. Gideon made an ephod thereof and put it in his city, even in Ophrah: and all Israel went thither a whoring after it, which thing became a snare unto Gideon, and to his house.

Thus was Midian subdued before the children of Israel, so that they lifted up their heads no more, and the country was in quietness forty years in the days of Gideon. Gideon had threescore and ten sons, for he had many wives, and his concubine in Shechem bare him a son whose name he called Abimelech; and Gideon the son of Joash died in a good old age. The sum of the history of Gideon, who is also named Jerubbaal, is this: the victory does not come in the strength of numbers, in how many guns or how many bullets you have. The victory of battle comes from the Lord, and that is why we have to trust in the Lord with all our heart and endure to the end, keeping these commandments until the return of our King of kings.

It came to pass, as soon as Gideon was dead, that the children of Israel turned again, and went a whoring after Baalim, and made Baal-berith their god, and remembered not the Lord their God, who had delivered them out of the hands of all their enemies on every side; neither shewed they kindness to the house of Jerubbaal. The same cycle turns again the moment the judge is gone. That is the whole lesson of the book: our deliverance is never our own hand, and our downfall is always our own forgetting. --- Topics: [Esau and Edom](/encyclopedia/esau-and-edom) · [Idolatry](/encyclopedia/idolatry) · [Sacrifice and Atonement](/encyclopedia/sacrifice-and-atonement) · [The Covenant](/encyclopedia/the-covenant) · [The Priesthood](/encyclopedia/the-priesthood)

Israel did evil in the sight of the Lord, and the Lord delivered them into the hand of Midian seven years. That is our manner: the Most High delivers us, we get a little bit of freedom, and we go right back to wickedness. The same thing goes on today; we get relaxed, and the Lord has to remind us, putting us right back into hard bondage, that this is not our rest. Because of the Midianites, the children of Israel made them the dens in the mountains, and caves, and strongholds; Israel hid in the mountains of their own land.

When Israel had sown, the Midianites, the Amalekites, and the children of the east came up as grasshoppers for multitude, destroyed the increase of the earth, and left no sustenance for Israel, neither sheep, nor ox, nor ass, and Israel was greatly impoverished. That goes right into the curses.

When Israel cried unto the Lord, the Lord sent a prophet to remind them: I brought you up from Egypt out of the house of bondage, and I said, fear not the gods of the Amorites in whose land ye dwell, but ye have not obeyed my voice. The judgment came with a reason attached.

An angel of the Lord came and sat under an oak in Ophrah, while Gideon threshed wheat by the winepress to hide it from the Midianites; that is how hard the oppression sat on the land, that a man hid his own harvest to keep it. The angel greets him: the Lord is with thee, thou mighty man of valour. The Most High already saw the warrior in the man hiding wheat.

Gideon answers, oh my Lord, if the Lord be with us, why then is all this befallen us, and where be all his miracles which our fathers told us of? A lot of us ask that same question today when we watch our people judged in the streets over and over: if we be the chosen people, why does all of this happen to us?

The Lord commissions him: go in this thy might, and thou shalt save Israel from the hand of the Midianites; have not I sent thee? Gideon answers with his pedigree: my family is poor in Manasseh, and I am the least in my father's house. That is a defeated mentality, and we all have to overcome it, because every one of us was called for a reason, to put a brick in for the kingdom.

The Lord promises, surely I will be with thee, and thou shalt smite the Midianites as one man. Gideon asks for a sign that it is really the Lord talking with him; the least in his father's house wanted to be sure he was not talking to himself.

Gideon brings a kid and unleavened cakes, and the angel touches the flesh and the cakes with the end of his staff; fire rises up out of the rock and consumes them, and the angel departs out of his sight, gone just like that. No lighter fluid existed on the earth; the angel made fire come out of the rock, because the angels are made out of that fire.

When Gideon perceived he had seen an angel of the Lord face to face, he feared death, but the Lord said, peace be unto thee; fear not: thou shalt not die. Gideon built an altar there and called it Jehovah-shalom, which is, the Lord is peace.

The same night the Lord tells him to throw down his own father's altar of Baal, cut down the grove by it, and build an altar unto the Lord in its place. Notice this: even before the split of the kingdom, the tribes that would become the northern kingdom were already dabbling with Baal, worshipping the Lord in some fashion while holding onto the idol.

In the morning the men of the city found the altar of Baal cast down, and when they inquired, they said, Gideon the son of Joash hath done this thing. He crept at night, but somebody was peeping out a window; he was doing the right thing and still got told on. The grove they worshipped was a carved tree stump, cut and shaped to look like a particular god; that is the idol Gideon cut down. The men demand his death, but Joash stands up for his son: will ye plead for Baal? If he be a god, let him plead for himself, because one hath cast down his altar. Obviously he is no god; he is an idol. So that day Gideon was named Jerubbaal, saying, let Baal plead against him.

The Midianites, the Amalekites, and the children of the east gathered and pitched in the valley of Jezreel, but the Spirit of the Lord came upon Gideon; he blew a trumpet, and Abiezer, Manasseh, Asher, Zebulun, and Naphtali came up to meet him. Those tribes are warriors; do not get it twisted. You see how Zebulun and Naphtali, who are in the south Americas right now, get down: that warrior spirit is still in them, only right now it has turned on each other, and the Most High is going to correct it and turn it right again.

Gideon asks the fleece signs: dew on the fleece only with dry earth beside, and then the reverse, dew on all the ground with the fleece dry. The Lord commands the dew, the condensation that falls through the night, to land exactly where he pleases; God can do whatever he wants, infinite power.

Abimelech was the son of Jerubbaal by his concubine in Shechem. He went to Shechem unto his mother's brethren, his uncles on his mother's side, and had them ask the men of Shechem whether it was better for all seventy sons of Jerubbaal to reign over them, or for one man to reign. Remember also that I am your bone and your flesh: he reminded them that he was family. When people do that, they want you to remember that blood is thicker than water, so you will back them whether or not it is right.

His mother's brethren spake of him in the ears of all the men of Shechem, whispering for their nephew, and their hearts inclined to follow Abimelech, for they said, He is our brother. They chose him by kinship, not by righteousness. They gave him threescore and ten pieces of silver out of the house of Baal-berith, money out of their idol's house to back his rise. Politics has always worked this way: people will put a man in office not because he is best for the job, but because he is family or because they know him. Baal was the chief god of the Canaanites, worshipped as the god of the elements who brought rain and made the ground fruitful, and sometimes as the god of war. Baal-berith, also called El-berith, was the Canaanite god of Shechem in the twelfth century BC, a sub god under Baal. With that money Abimelech hired vain and light persons, wicked and empty men, which followed him.

He went unto his father's house at Ophrah and slew his brethren the sons of Jerubbaal, threescore and ten persons, upon one stone. He killed his own family to clear his way to a throne. Notwithstanding, Jotham the youngest son of Jerubbaal was left, for he hid himself.

All the men of Shechem and all the house of Millo gathered together and made Abimelech king by the plain of the pillar that was in Shechem. They endorsed the man who had just used their money and his hired men to murder his seventy brothers.

When they told it to Jotham, he went and stood in the top of mount Gerizim, lifted up his voice, and cried, Hearken unto me, ye men of Shechem, that God may hearken unto you. This young brother was fearless; he stood up alone and rebuked the men who had made his brothers' killer king. In his parable the trees went forth on a time to anoint a king over them. The olive tree would not leave its fatness, wherewith by it they honour God and man; the fig tree would not forsake its sweetness and good fruit; the vine would not leave its wine, which cheereth God and man. The profitable trees refused to be promoted over the trees. Only the bramble accepted: if in truth ye anoint me king over you, then come and put your trust in my shadow; and if not, let fire come out of the bramble and devour the cedars of Lebanon. The worthless bush took the crown, and its answer carried the threat of fire.

Jotham applied the parable: if ye have done truly and sincerely in that ye have made Abimelech king, and if ye have dealt well with Jerubbaal and his house, then rejoice ye in Abimelech, and let him also rejoice in you. He reminded them of what they owed his father: my father fought for you, and adventured his life far, and delivered you out of the hand of Midian; and ye are risen up against my father's house this day, and have slain his sons, threescore and ten persons upon one stone, and have made Abimelech, the son of his maidservant, king over the men of Shechem, because he is your brother. They did it only because he was kin to them. But if not, let fire come out from Abimelech and devour the men of Shechem and the house of Millo; and let fire come out from the men of Shechem and from the house of Millo, and devour Abimelech. That is what the parable of the bramble was about: he prophesied that they would destroy one another, and it came to pass.
Jotham ran away and fled to Beer and dwelt there, for fear of Abimelech his brother. His brother already had a reputation for killing; he knew he could be next.

When Abimelech had reigned three years over Israel, God sent an evil spirit between Abimelech and the men of Shechem, and the men of Shechem dealt treacherously with Abimelech. Read that carefully: the Lord sent the evil spirit. When somebody's spirit suddenly changes toward you, we tend to think it is just that person; the scripture shows the Most High is the one who stirs these things. War and strife between nations are not coincidence, karma, or mother nature; those are the world's false ideas and idols. The Most High is in the midst of these things, mustering the host, the armies above and below, and he even puts it on the spirit of one wicked man to go against another. The reason is given: that the cruelty done to the threescore and ten sons of Jerubbaal might come, and their blood be laid upon Abimelech their brother, which slew them, and upon the men of Shechem, which aided him in the killing of his brethren. The hired men and the backers carried the blood guilt too. Abimelech ran for three years and everything looked good, but you are not getting away with evil.
The men of Shechem set liers in wait for him in the top of the mountains, and they robbed all that came along that way by them; and it was told Abimelech. The treachery the Most High sent had begun.

Gaal the son of Ebed came with his brethren and went over to Shechem, and the men of Shechem put their confidence in him. They went out into the fields, gathered their vineyards, trode the grapes, made merry, went into the house of their god, did eat and drink, and cursed Abimelech. Gaal talked big: who is Abimelech, and who is Shechem, that we should serve him? is not he the son of Jerubbaal? and Zebul his officer? serve the men of Hamor the father of Shechem: for why should we serve him? He asked why they should be serving this Israelite at all. Would to God this people were under my hand! then would I remove Abimelech. He was talking cash money with wine in him: increase thine army, and come out.

When Zebul the ruler of the city, Abimelech's officer, heard the words of Gaal the son of Ebed, his anger was kindled. He sent messengers unto Abimelech privily, saying, Behold, Gaal and his brethren fortify the city against thee. Zebul counselled Abimelech to rise up by night with his people and lie in wait in the field, and in the morning, as soon as the sun was up, to set upon the city. This is the same hand we read of in verse 23; the Lord is in the midst of this whole treachery, turning it back on all of them.

Abimelech and all the people with him rose up by night and laid wait against Shechem in four companies. When Gaal saw the people coming down from the top of the mountains, Zebul told him, Thou seest the shadow of the mountains as if they were men, playing him until it was too late. Then Zebul threw his own words back at him: where is now thy mouth, wherewith thou saidst, Who is Abimelech, that we should serve him? is not this the people that thou hast despised? go out, I pray now, and fight with them. All of that big talk disappeared when the fight showed up. Gaal went out before the men of Shechem and fought with Abimelech, and Abimelech chased him, and he fled before him, and many were overthrown and wounded, even unto the entering of the gate. Abimelech dwelt at Arumah, and Zebul thrust out Gaal and his brethren, that they should not dwell in Shechem.

On the morrow the people went out into the field, and it was told Abimelech. He divided his men into three companies, laid wait in the field, rose up against the people, and smote them. Abimelech fought against the city all that day; he took the city, slew the people that was therein, beat down the city, and sowed it with salt.

When all the men of the tower of Shechem heard that, they entered into an hold of the house of the god Berith. Abimelech gat him up to mount Zalmon, cut down a bough from the trees with an axe, laid it on his shoulder, and said unto the people that were with him, What ye have seen me do, make haste, and do as I have done. They cut every man his bough, put them to the hold, and set the hold on fire upon them, so that all the men of the tower of Shechem died also, about a thousand men and women. Remember, these are the people whose money and endorsement made him king: I am your brother, make me king. Now he turned on Shechem itself and burned them; the fire out of the bramble that Jotham prophesied was devouring the men of Shechem.

Then went Abimelech to Thebez, and there was a strong tower within the city, and all the men and women of the city fled to the top of it. Abimelech came unto the tower and went hard unto the door to burn it with fire, and a certain woman cast a piece of a millstone upon Abimelech's head, and all to brake his skull. A millstone is a heavy stone; it crushed his skull. He called hastily unto the young man his armourbearer: draw thy sword, and slay me, that men say not of me, A woman slew him. It was counted a shame for a man of war to die by the hand of a woman, as when Jael put Sisera to death earlier in this book. His young man thrust him through, and he died. He reigned only three years. Killing his seventy brothers bought him a three year reign and a crushed skull; it was to no profit. If you are doing wickedness behind closed doors and think the Most High does not see it, he sees it, and he brings swift judgment.

Thus God rendered the wickedness of Abimelech, which he did unto his father, in slaying his seventy brethren; and all the evil of the men of Shechem did God render upon their heads. Both sides were judged; for three years they reigned and everything looked good, then the Most High brought the judgment. Upon them came the curse of Jotham the son of Jerubbaal. Our forefather Jotham, a young man at the time, prophesied their destruction, and it came to pass. We read these accounts for the history, but look deeper and apply them to our lives: if there is evil being done behind closed doors, the Most High will judge it in front of everybody, like he judged Abimelech.

An image in itself is not the sin, except for that white image of the beast; making images to bow down to them and serve them is the transgression, for the Lord thy God is a jealous God. Visiting the iniquity of the fathers upon the children unto the third and fourth generation: Israel is yet this day in captivity, scattered for a reproach and a curse, according to all the iniquities of the fathers which departed from the Lord. Right now Israel is paying for the sins of the fathers; that is why the people are scattered to the four corners of the earth.

And shewing mercy unto thousands of them that love me, and keep my commandments. Judith recounted how the Most High tried the fathers for the examination of their hearts: he tried Abraham and Isaac, and Jacob in Mesopotamia of Syria keeping the sheep of Laban, serving twenty years with his wages changed and given Leah when he looked for Rachel. In Judith's day there was no tribe, family, people, nor city that worshipped gods made with hands, as had been aforetime; for that cause she trusted the Lord would not despise the nation. Mercy rests on them that know none other God, not Allah, not Buddha, not a white Jesus.

Remember the Sabbath day, to keep it holy. The word says remember because Israel would forget it: in this captivity the people were forced to serve other gods and their religions, and the Sabbath was lost through forced conversion. Look up the blue laws, also known as Sunday laws; they help give understanding of why the Bible says remember the Sabbath day.

An altar of stone was not to be built of hewn stone, for lifting up a tool upon it pollutes it; neither go up by steps unto the altar, that thy nakedness be not discovered thereon. This scripture helps explain pants, precept upon precept. The priests were given linen breeches to cover their nakedness from the loins even unto the thighs when they came near the altar, and Israel was called in this same reading to be a kingdom of priests, so do not be simple and say that law was only for Aaron and his sons. Those breeches were made for men and not for women, as the law of the garments also shows.

verses.text: Then the men of Israel said unto Gideon, Rule thou over us, both thou, and thy son, and thy son’s son also: for thou hast delivered us from the hand of Midian.
And Gideon said unto them, I will not rule over you, neither shall my son rule over you: the Lord shall rule over you.
And Gideon said unto them, I would desire a request of you, that ye would give me every man the earrings of his prey. (For they had golden earrings, because they were Ishmaelites.)
And they answered, We will willingly give them. And they spread a garment, and did cast therein every man the earrings of his prey.

And the weight of the golden earrings that he requested was a thousand and seven hundred shekels of gold; beside ornaments, and collars, and purple raiment that was on the kings of Midian, and beside the chains that were about their camels’ necks.
And Gideon made an ephod thereof, and put it in his city, even in Ophrah: and all Israel went thither a whoring after it: which thing became a snare unto Gideon, and to his house.
And it came to pass, as soon as Gideon was dead, that the children of Israel turned again, and went a whoring after Baalim, and made Baal–berith their god.
And the children of Israel remembered not the Lord their God, who had delivered them out of the hands of all their enemies on every side:
Neither shewed they kindness to the house of Jerubbaal, namely, Gideon, according to all the goodness which he had shewed unto Israel.

And it came to pass the same night, that the Lord said unto him, Take thy father’s young bullock, even the second bullock of seven years old, and throw down the altar of Baal that thy father hath, and cut down the grove that is by it:

And build an altar unto the Lord thy God upon the top of this rock, in the ordered place, and take the second bullock, and offer a burnt sacrifice with the wood of the grove which thou shalt cut down.

Then Gideon took ten men of his servants, and did as the Lord had said unto him: and so it was, because he feared his father’s household, and the men of the city, that he could not do it by day, that he did it by night.

And he went unto his father’s house at Ophrah, and slew his brethren the sons of Jerubbaal, being threescore and ten persons, upon one stone: notwithstanding yet Jotham the youngest son of Jerubbaal was left; for he hid himself.
Ye shall not make with me gods of silver, neither shall ye make unto you gods of gold.

lawsResolved.text: You shall not make for yourself or erect any graven image, idol, molten god, or likeness of anything to worship.
You shall not bring a graven image or other such abomination into your house.
Do not set up idols in your heart, for it will cause you to stumble into iniquity.
The proper vestures to be worn by a priest.

text.text: Then the men of Israel said unto Gideon, Rule thou over us, both thou, and thy son, and thy son’s son also: for thou hast delivered us from the hand of Midian.
And Gideon said unto them, I will not rule over you, neither shall my son rule over you: the Lord shall rule over you.
And Gideon said unto them, I would desire a request of you, that ye would give me every man the earrings of his prey. (For they had golden earrings, because they were Ishmaelites.)
And they answered, We will willingly give them. And they spread a garment, and did cast therein every man the earrings of his prey.

And the weight of the golden earrings that he requested was a thousand and seven hundred shekels of gold; beside ornaments, and collars, and purple raiment that was on the kings of Midian, and beside the chains that were about their camels’ necks.
And Gideon made an ephod thereof, and put it in his city, even in Ophrah: and all Israel went thither a whoring after it: which thing became a snare unto Gideon, and to his house.
And it came to pass, as soon as Gideon was dead, that the children of Israel turned again, and went a whoring after Baalim, and made Baal–berith their god.
And the children of Israel remembered not the Lord their God, who had delivered them out of the hands of all their enemies on every side:
Neither shewed they kindness to the house of Jerubbaal, namely, Gideon, according to all the goodness which he had shewed unto Israel.

And it came to pass the same night, that the Lord said unto him, Take thy father’s young bullock, even the second bullock of seven years old, and throw down the altar of Baal that thy father hath, and cut down the grove that is by it:

And build an altar unto the Lord thy God upon the top of this rock, in the ordered place, and take the second bullock, and offer a burnt sacrifice with the wood of the grove which thou shalt cut down.

Then Gideon took ten men of his servants, and did as the Lord had said unto him: and so it was, because he feared his father’s household, and the men of the city, that he could not do it by day, that he did it by night.

And he went unto his father’s house at Ophrah, and slew his brethren the sons of Jerubbaal, being threescore and ten persons, upon one stone: notwithstanding yet Jotham the youngest son of Jerubbaal was left; for he hid himself.
Ye shall not make with me gods of silver, neither shall ye make unto you gods of gold.
